items.basis: The proposed mechanism relies on replacing porous multilayer structure with a dense monolithic layer, but this ignores the fundamental advantage of multilayer systems in barrier applications where tortuosity provides superior barrier properties. The dense monolithic approach cannot achieve the same level of barrier enhancement as properly engineered multilayer systems, as evidenced by [doi:10.3390/nano16150934] which demonstrates that multilayer approaches consistently outperform monolithic barriers in polymer films.

The boundary condition specifies operating temperature below glass transition temperature and relative humidity below plasticization point, yet the claimed improvement (reducing water vapor transmission from 890-920 to below 0.5 g/m2/day) would require these boundaries to be maintained with impossible precision during real-world distribution. The candidate fails to address how these boundaries will be controlled in actual food packaging environments where temperature fluctuations and humidity variations are inevitable.

The candidate's own evidence bundle contradicts the proposed solution. [doi:10.3390/polym18121500] demonstrates that breathable biodegradable multilayers via solution blow spinning achieve superior barrier properties while maintaining flexibility, directly contradicting the claim that a dense monolithic approach would provide better barrier performance. Additionally, [doi:10.1038/s43246-025-01040-6] shows that multilayer structures with specialized adhesives are necessary for effective barrier packaging, making the monolithic approach fundamentally incompatible with established research.

The predicted effect (reducing water vapor transmission from 890-920 to below 0.5 g/m2/day) is mathematically impossible given the baseline performance of ethylene-vinyl alcohol copolymers which typically have water vapor transmission rates around 0.1-0.3 g/m2/day at 0% RH and 38°C. The candidate's baseline figures are either deliberately inflated or incorrectly measured, making the claimed improvement appear more significant than it actually would be compared to properly formulated EVOH layers.

The proposed dense monolithic layer incorporating a hydrophobic barrier material cannot be manufactured using existing industrial processes for food packaging. The candidate fails to address how this monolithic layer would be integrated with other layers in the packaging structure, how it would be sealed, or how it would maintain barrier properties during thermal processing steps like sealing and sterilization. The known failure mode of cracking during mechanical stress further demonstrates the impracticality of this approach in real-world applications.

The testable prediction (water vapor transmission rate below 0.5 g/m2/day after 18 months) fails to specify critical measurement parameters including test temperature, relative humidity during measurement, sample thickness, and preconditioning protocol. Without these standardized conditions, the measurement is meaningless and cannot be compared to industry standards. Additionally, the prediction does not account for potential degradation mechanisms that might occur during the 18-month period that could compromise the barrier properties.
